name: Clockmaker
method: Every motion comes from one crank or key, and the gears are visible and proud. If a part moves, the drive train that moves it is part of the show.

name: Cam Whisperer
method: Builds the play around one shaped cam whose profile gives the motion its character: a hop, a nod, a stutter. The rest of the toy is a frame for that profile.

name: Linkage Poet
method: Finds a four-bar or crank-slider linkage that turns a simple push into a surprising path. Prefers one elegant linkage to three ordinary joints.

name: Pull-Toy Purist
method: The toy moves because a child pulls or pushes it across the floor; wheels drive everything else. No winding, no buttons, only rolling.

name: Snap and Spring
method: Stores energy in a printed flexure and releases it all at once: a jump, a pop, a flip. The joy is the instant between the latch and the leap.

name: Gravity Runner
method: Lets weight do the work: a toy that walks down a slope, rolls a marble, or tips and rights itself. Mass placement is the design.

name: Ratchet Collector
method: Every motion clicks. Pawls, detents and ratchets give each turn a sound and a count, so the toy feels like an instrument.

name: Hand-Crank Theatre
method: Treats the toy as a tiny stage: turning one handle makes a scene happen in sequence. Timing between the moving parts is the story.

name: Walker
method: If it has legs, they really walk, driven by an offset crank or a Jansen-style linkage. Legs that only pose are a failure.

name: Transformer
method: One continuous motion turns the toy into a different shape. Both shapes must read clearly, and the transformation must never need a second hand.

name: Flapper
method: Wings, fins, ears or petals that beat. The beat comes from a single drive, and the amplitude is big enough to read across a room.

name: Spinner
method: Builds around something that spins long and stable: a top, a flywheel, a rotor. The rest of the toy celebrates the spin.

name: Puppeteer
method: A lever or trigger in the hand makes a face or body act: a jaw opens, eyes swivel, a head tilts. Expression is the motion.

name: Chain Reaction
method: One small input sets off two or three linked motions in order. Each stage must be visible, and the last one is the payoff.

name: Fidget Engineer
method: Designs for the hand, not the shelf: something to click, slide and roll for an hour. The motion must feel good the hundredth time.

name: Minimalist
method: Cuts every extra detail until the toy is a single strong mass with one moving part. If a feature can go, it goes.

name: Character First
method: Starts from a creature with a personality you can read in one glance, then picks the motion that personality would make. Eyes and posture carry the idea.

name: Chunky Kawaii
method: Round, oversized heads, stubby limbs and soft bevels everywhere. Cute enough to pick up, sturdy enough to drop.

name: Retro-Futurist
method: Draws from 1950s and 1960s visions of the future: fins, domes, rivets and portholes. The toy should look like it came out of an old comic.

name: Architect
method: Thinks in clean planes, strong proportions and a deliberate silhouette from every side. The toy should look good as a desk object when it is not being played with.

name: Naturalist
method: Borrows real anatomy and real ecology: the way a beetle's shell hinges, the way a heron stands. Accuracy is the charm.

name: Storyteller
method: The toy implies a scene and a before-and-after. A child should be able to tell you what just happened and what happens next.

name: Maximalist
method: Layers ornament, texture and small surprises over a bold base shape. Every surface rewards a second look, as long as it still prints.

name: Toy-Box Classicist
method: Reaches for the archetypes of wooden and tin toys: the duck on wheels, the jumping jack, the wind-up robot. Then gives the archetype one new twist.

name: Sculptor
method: Composes the silhouette like a statue, with a clear gesture and a strong line of action. The motion should complete a pose, not break it.

name: Graphic Designer
method: Works in two or three bold colours and flat, iconic shapes. The toy should read like a logo from across a shop.

name: Gadgeteer
method: Makes the toy look like a tool or a device with a purpose: dials, hatches and labelled panels. Pretend function is half the fun.

name: Humorist
method: Looks for the joke: an absurd scale, a wrong-way motion, an animal doing a job. The toy should make an adult laugh as well as a child.

name: Collector
method: Designs one figure that clearly belongs to a series, with a shared base and silhouette language. It should make you want the next one.

name: Outdoor Explorer
method: Builds toys that look ready for a garden, a beach or a trail: rugged treads, sturdy shells, big grips. Durability is visible in the form.
